newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: SIA raises air fares by three percent.
newsitem.headline: SIA raises air fares by three percent.

text.p: Singapore Airlines Ltd (SIA) has raised international passenger air fares by three percent, a company spokesman said on Monday.

"Owing to the rise in fuel prices and the attendant cost burden experienced by the airline industry, SIA has raised airfares by three percent as of December 15, 1996," the spokesman said in response to a Reuters query.
SIA said in November it would increase fares, but did not say when.

"During the first half of the current financial year (April- September) SIA's fuel costs increased by 22 percent over the corresponding period of the previous year," the company said in November. "SIA experienced a net Singapore $83 million increase in its fuel bill."
The spokesman said on Monday there had been no formal announcement of the fare increase.
The increase was in line with a recommendation issued by the International Air Transport Association (IATA) on November 15 due to big increases in fuel oil costs.
The 251-member IATA proposed a global three percent fare increase to make up for a more than 40 percent rise in fuel costs this year.
Several other Asian carriers including Japan Airlines Ltd, All Nippon Airways Co Ltd, Malaysian Airlines and Cathay Pacific Airways Ltd have either raised or plan to raise fares.
Fuel represents around 10 percent of most airlines' costs.
In Asia, as measured by benchmark Singapore prices, jet fuel prices rose about 25 percent in 1996 from year-earlier levels to an average of around $28.50 per barrel.
Jet fuel prices are currently assessed at around $33.50 per barrel on a free-on-board Singapore basis.
Oil traders said prices were unlikely to fall substantially over the next few weeks as winter demand from Japan and South Korea for heating oil was not expected to ease until sometime in February.
Jet fuel is also used for heating and lighting as kerosene.
One trader said demand had picked up from Indonesia and China ahead of holidays in those countries.

Indonesia had bought around two million barrels of jet fuel for January arrival ahead of the Ramadan holidays, while China had bought about one million barrels for arrival prior to the Lunar New Year holidays.
The purchases are 10 to 30 percent more than the usual monthly demand from the two countries, traders said.
